title: Review: Stem cells; Gas exchange surfaces and SA:V in organisms; Human gas exchange and ventilation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EX02a#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX02a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX01b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CE08b#N.5, EX01a#N.10, EX01b#N.5, EX02a#N.11, EX01a#N.11a, EX01b#N.3, EX02a#N.6, EX01a#N.7a, EX01b#N.11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Surfactant
items.clue: Substance in the moist lining of the air sacs that stops them collapsing

items.label: Diaphragm
items.clue: Muscle below the lungs that contracts, flattens and moves down when breathing in

items.label: Alveoli
items.clue: Air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles: the only place where gases are exchanged

items.label: Fick's law
items.clue: Diffusion rate is proportional to area × difference in concentration, divided by thickness

questions.stem: Bone marrow transplants are used to treat leukaemia. Which statement explains how a transplant replaces the patient's blood cells?

options.text: The donor marrow's stem cells can become any body cell, so they replace any damaged tissue.
Mature red blood cells in the donor marrow divide to make all the new blood cells.
Donor stem cells divide and differentiate to give every type of blood cell.
Donor white blood cells switch into red blood cells when the patient needs more.

questions.explanation: Blood stem cells renew themselves and differentiate into red cells, white cells and platelet-forming cells, rebuilding the patient's blood supply.

questions.stem: Use the data on the mouse, human and elephant. Which statement is supported by the data?

options.text: The mouse uses more energy each day than the elephant, since its rate per kg is far higher.
Each kg of body uses energy at about the same rate in all three, so total use is proportional to mass.
Each kg of mouse uses energy about 13 times as fast as each kg of elephant.
The elephant has the highest rate per kg, because its greater surface area loses more heat.

questions.explanation: 720 ÷ 56 ≈ 13. The small mouse has a high SA:V, loses heat fast per kg, and so respires fast per kg.

questions.stem: Suppose that blood flow through the gill capillaries of an anaesthetised fish is stopped while water continues to flow over the gills, and that oxygen uptake across the gills falls almost to zero within a minute. Which explanation is best supported?

options.text: With no blood flow, oxygen built up in the stationary blood until its concentration matched the water's, so the gradient was lost.
Stopping blood flow cannot affect the gradient across the gill; the water flowing over the gills must have run out of oxygen.
Blood held still in the capillaries should load more fully, so the fall must have been caused by damage to the gill surface.
Oxygen enters with water absorbed into the blood, and once the blood stopped moving no more water could be taken up.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?

options.text: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.

questions.explanation: Larger thorax volume, pressure in the lungs below atmospheric, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

questions.stem: An amoeba gets all its oxygen by diffusion across its cell-surface membrane. Why could a mouse not get enough oxygen by diffusion across its body surface alone?

options.text: A mouse has a smaller total surface area than an amoeba, so less oxygen can cross into its body.
A mouse has a much lower SA:V, and most of its cells lie too far from its surface for diffusion to supply them.
A mouse's cells are each much larger than an amoeba's cell, so every cell needs more oxygen than diffusion delivers.
Diffusion of oxygen can happen only in water, so a mouse on land cannot use it at any surface.

questions.stem: A model exchange surface is changed. Its surface area is doubled and its thickness is tripled. The difference in concentration does not change. By what factor does the rate of diffusion change?
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ area ÷ thickness here, so the factor is 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67. The extra thickness outweighs the extra area.

questions.stem: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?

options.text: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.

questions.stem: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?

options.text: The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.

questions.explanation: Proportionally less surface supplies each unit of volume, and inner cells are too far away for diffusion alone. Both make specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

questions.stem: Lungless salamanders have no lungs and, as adults, no gills. They exchange gases across their skin and the lining of the mouth. Which set of features would best suit this way of life?

options.text: Dry, thick skin, so that gases cross it as gases without having to dissolve first.
Thin, moist skin over a dense capillary network, with blood flowing through it continuously.
A large, bulky body, so that the total area of skin available for gas exchange is as large as possible.
Slow blood flow through the skin, so that each red blood cell has time to fill with oxygen.
